html:
The Northern Crusades were wars of conquest and forced conversion waged by Catholic kingdoms and military orders against the pagan peoples around the Baltic Sea, from the 1100s to the 1300s. The popes granted them the same status as crusades to the Holy Land.

They began with the Wendish Crusade of 1147 against the Slavs east of the Elbe. Around 1200 German merchants and churchmen moved into Livonia: Bishop Albert founded Riga in 1201 and set up a military order, the Sword Brothers. With Danish help they conquered the Livonians, Latvians and Ests by the 1220s. Sweden led its own campaigns into Finland.

From 1230 the Teutonic Knights turned to the Prussians, whom they conquered after fifty years of hard war, and they took over the Sword Brothers' lands. Their crusader state ruled the coast from Prussia to Estonia. German nobles, clergy and townsmen formed its ruling class for centuries, while the native Baltic and Finnic peoples became peasants. The Old Prussian language died out.

Lithuania held out longest. Its grand duke Jogaila became king of Poland and was baptised with his people in 1387, which took away the crusade's reason. The Polish-Lithuanian army crushed the Teutonic Knights at Grunwald in 1410.
